OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Vaginal Blee:
Vaginal bleeding in pregnancy is a presenting complaint, not a diagnosis — the first question is always the gestation. In early pregnancy (<24 weeks) the can’t-miss cause is an ectopic pregnancy, and the commonest is miscarriage (see early pregnancy complications). After 24 weeks bleeding is an antepartum haemorrhage (APH) — the two dangerous causes are placenta praevia (classically painless) and placental abruption (classically painful, with a tense, tender uterus) (see antepartum haemorrhage & placental disorders). Always confirm the pregnancy and gestation, assess maternal haemodynamics and fetal wellbeing, and check the rhesus status. Local causes (cervical ectropion, polyp, a “bloody show” of labour) are common but a diagnosis of exclusion (see benign cervical conditions). Bleeding often comes with pain (see abdominal pain in pregnancy).
🚨Never perform a digital vaginal examination in suspected placenta praevia — it can provoke catastrophic haemorrhage; localise the placenta on ultrasound first (see antepartum haemorrhage). In early pregnancy, a positive test with bleeding and pain is an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise (see early pregnancy complications) — a ruptured ectopic can cause collapse from occult intra-abdominal bleeding. Treat significant APH as an obstetric emergency: A–E resuscitation, senior obstetric help and neonatal alert. Give anti-D to non-sensitised rhesus-negative women after a potentially sensitising bleed (any bleeding ≥12 weeks, or <12 weeks if heavy / painful or surgically managed, and for ectopic or molar pregnancy), and continuous CTG if the fetus is viable.

  • Threatened (bleeding, closed os, viable fetus) vs inevitable / incomplete (open os, products, pain)

  • Uterus large-for-dates, very high hCG, exaggerated symptoms

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Abdominal Pa:
Abdominal pain in pregnancy is a presenting complaint whose differential turns on the gestation and on whether the cause is obstetric or non-obstetric. In early pregnancy the priority is to exclude an ectopic pregnancy (see early pregnancy complications). In later pregnancy the dangerous obstetric causes are placental abruption, pre-eclampsia / HELLP (epigastric or right-upper-quadrant pain) and labour — and, on a scarred uterus, uterine rupture (see placental disorders, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy). Pregnancy does not protect against surgical disease: appendicitis is the commonest non-obstetric surgical emergency and the pain is often higher and atypical as the gravid uterus displaces the appendix (see acute appendicitis). Always confirm the gestation, assess mother and fetus, and check the blood pressure and urine. Pain often accompanies bleeding (see vaginal bleeding in pregnancy).
🚨Four obstetric emergencies hide in abdominal pain: a ruptured ectopic (early, with collapse), placental abruption (constant pain, a tense “woody” tender uterus ± bleeding), pre-eclampsia / HELLP (epigastric / RUQ pain with hypertension — check BP and urine) (see hypertensive disorders of pregnancy), and uterine rupture on a scarred uterus (see intrapartum emergencies). Do not attribute pain to labour without examining and monitoring the fetus (CTG). And do not miss appendicitis — delayed surgery in pregnancy raises perforation, fetal loss and maternal mortality. Assess mother and fetus together, and resuscitate early.

  • Positive test + unilateral pelvic pain ± bleeding in early pregnancy

🟠Placental abruption
  • Constant pain + tense, tender “woody” uterus ± vaginal bleeding
  • Fetal distress; bleeding may be concealed (see placental disorders)
  • Clinical diagnosis — ultrasound may be normal; resuscitate

  • Regular, painful tightenings with cervical change ± a “show” or ruptured membranes

  • Appendicitis — pain often higher / atypical, with anorexia and fever (see acute appendicitis)

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Reduced Feta:
Reduced fetal movements (RFM) is one of the most important presentations in obstetrics because it may be the only warning of fetal compromise or impending stillbirth. Movements are usually felt from around 18–24 weeks, and there is no defined normal number — what matters is a reduction from the woman’s own established pattern (see reduced fetal movements). The overriding rule is to never dismiss it: many women with RFM have a healthy baby, but a subset have placental insufficiency and fetal growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, abruption, fetomaternal haemorrhage or, at worst, an intrauterine death (see hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, placental disorders). Assessment is urgent: confirm the fetal heart, then CTG and, where indicated, ultrasound growth and Doppler (see antenatal care). RFM may accompany bleeding or pain (see vaginal bleeding in pregnancy).
🚨Reduced fetal movements can be the first — and only — sign of an unwell or dying baby. The immediate priority is to confirm the fetal heartbeat with a handheld Doppler; if no heartbeat is detected, arrange an urgent real-time ultrasound to confirm or exclude an intrauterine death — do not simply reassure (see reduced fetal movements). If a heartbeat is present, perform CTG (from around 26–28 weeks); an abnormal trace, a small-for-dates uterus or associated bleeding / hypertension mandates senior review and consideration of delivery (see placental disorders). Recurrent RFM carries a higher risk of adverse outcome and warrants heightened surveillance.

🚩Intrauterine fetal death
  • No fetal heartbeat detectable on handheld Doppler
  • → urgent real-time ultrasound to confirm absent cardiac activity (see reduced fetal movements)
  • Do not simply reassure — RFM may be the presenting sign of death
🚩Acute fetal compromise
  • Abnormal CTG — reduced variability, decelerations, or a sinusoidal trace
  • Consider abruption, cord accident or acute hypoxia (see placental disorders)
  • Senior obstetric review; consider urgent delivery
🟠Placental insufficiency & FGR
  • Chronic uteroplacental insufficiency → fetal growth restriction, the commonest serious cause
  • Small-for-dates uterus, oligohydramnios, abnormal umbilical artery Doppler (see hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
  • Risk factors: pre-eclampsia, smoking, diabetes, previous FGR / stillbirth
🟠Reduced perception
  • Fetal sleep cycle, anterior placenta, maternal position or raised BMI, early gestation
  • Common and benign — but a diagnosis of exclusion after a normal CTG ± scan (see reduced fetal movements)
  • Safety-net: return immediately if movements reduce again
🩹Fetomaternal haemorrhage
  • Fetal blood loss into the maternal circulation → fetal anaemia
  • A sinusoidal CTG or a recent sensitising event is a clue (see reduced fetal movements)
  • Diagnose with a Kleihauer test; may need transfusion / delivery
🩹Infection & other causes
  • Congenital infection (e.g. CMV, parvovirus) or maternal febrile illness (see infections in pregnancy)
  • Oligohydramnios, cord problems, congenital anomaly
  • Guided by the CTG and ultrasound findings

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__PV Discharge:
Vaginal discharge is extremely common and usually physiological — the task is to separate normal from the infective, and to spot the sinister. Characterise the discharge by colour, consistency, odour, itch and pain. The three commonest infective causes are bacterial vaginosis (thin grey, fishy odour), candidiasis (thick white, itchy) and trichomoniasis (frothy green) (see bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis). Discharge from cervicitis — chlamydia and gonorrhoea — may be the gateway to pelvic inflammatory disease, which threatens fertility (see chlamydia, pelvic inflammatory disease). Always take a sexual history, do a pregnancy test, and never dismiss a persistent, offensive or blood-stained discharge, which can signal malignancy (see gynaecological cancers). See also the shared discharge approach (see urethral / vaginal discharge).
🚨Do not miss pelvic inflammatory disease, cancer, toxic shock or ruptured membranes. Discharge with deep dyspareunia, pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness or fever is PID — treat empirically on a low threshold to protect fertility (see pelvic inflammatory disease). A persistent, offensive, watery or blood-stained discharge with post-coital or intermenstrual bleeding needs a speculum and urgent referral for cervical or endometrial cancer (see gynaecological cancers). A retained tampon or foreign body with fever, rash and hypotension is toxic shock. In pregnancy, a watery gush may be ruptured membranes (see preterm birth & PPROM).

  • Thin, grey-white, homogeneous discharge with a fishy odour, minimal itch

  • Treat with metronidazole; associated with preterm birth in pregnancy

  • Thick white “cottage cheese” discharge with vulval itch and soreness
  • Normal pH; spores / pseudohyphae on microscopy (see candidiasis)

  • Mucopurulent cervicitis; often asymptomatic, or discharge with IMB / PCB / dysuria
  • Commonest STIs; risk of ascending PID (see chlamydia, gonorrhoea)

  • Frothy yellow-green offensive discharge, vulval soreness, strawberry cervix
  • Sexually transmitted protozoan; test and treat the partner (see pelvic & vaginal infections)
  • Also physiological discharge, atrophic vaginitis, dermatoses (see anogenital itch / rash)

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Amenorrhoea:
Amenorrhoea is the absence of menstruation, and the first rule is simple: always exclude pregnancy. Divide it into primary (no menses by 15 with secondary sexual characteristics, or by 13 without) and secondary (established periods stopping for ≥3–6 months) (see menstrual disorders). The commonest cause of secondary amenorrhoea is pregnancy; the rest are largely endocrine — PCOS, hypothalamic amenorrhoea (low weight, exercise, stress), hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease and premature ovarian insufficiency (see PCOS, hyperprolactinaemia, menopause & fertility). Primary amenorrhoea adds genetic and structural causes — Turner’s, outflow obstruction and androgen insensitivity (see androgen insensitivity syndrome). Amenorrhoea often overlaps with subfertility (see subfertility).
🚨Do a pregnancy test first — and think of the pituitary. Pregnancy (including an ectopic) is the commonest cause of secondary amenorrhoea (see early pregnancy complications). Do not miss a prolactinoma or other pituitary tumour: galactorrhoea, headache and a bitemporal visual-field defect demand serum prolactin and pituitary imaging (see hyperprolactinaemia, galactorrhoea). Premature ovarian insufficiency (amenorrhoea with a raised FSH under 40) needs HRT to protect bone and cardiovascular health (see menopause & fertility). In primary amenorrhoea, cyclical pain with a bulging membrane is an obstructed outflow tract needing surgery.

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Heavy Menstr:
Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) is excessive menstrual loss that interferes with a woman’s physical, social or emotional quality of life — it is defined by its impact, not a millilitre threshold. Structure the causes with PALM-COEIN: the structural PALM (polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma / fibroid, malignancy & hyperplasia) and the non-structural COEIN (coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial, iatrogenic, not otherwise classified) (see menstrual disorders, benign uterine conditions). Always exclude pregnancy and assess for anaemia. The can’t-miss causes are endometrial or cervical cancer / hyperplasia (see gynaecological cancers) and, especially in adolescents, an underlying bleeding disorder (see von Willebrand disease). HMB may accompany painful periods (see dysmenorrhoea) or bleeding between periods (see intermenstrual / post-coital bleeding).
🚨Do not miss endometrial cancer, a bleeding disorder or anaemia. HMB with intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding, or in a woman over 45 or with risk factors (obesity, PCOS, tamoxifen, unopposed oestrogen, Lynch syndrome), warrants endometrial assessment — TVUS and biopsy — to exclude cancer or hyperplasia (see gynaecological cancers). HMB since menarche, with easy bruising or a family history, suggests von Willebrand disease or another coagulopathy (see von Willebrand disease). Severe or chronic bleeding causes symptomatic iron-deficiency anaemia — check the FBC and ferritin and treat (see anaemia).

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Intermenstru:
Intermenstrual bleeding (IMB, between periods) and post-coital bleeding (PCB, after intercourse) share one overriding rule: exclude cervical and endometrial cancer. PCB is the classic symptom of cervical cancer, and a normal-looking cervix does not exclude it (see gynaecological cancers). The common benign causes are cervical ectropion, cervical or endometrial polyps, cervicitis from chlamydia, and breakthrough bleeding on hormonal contraception (see benign cervical conditions, chlamydia, contraception counselling). Always exclude pregnancy, check the cervical screening history, take a sexual history, and inspect the cervix with a speculum. In perimenopause, consider atrophic vaginitis (see menopause & fertility); bleeding after the menopause is a separate red-flag presentation (see postmenopausal bleeding).
🚨Post-coital bleeding is cervical cancer until proven otherwise, and a normal-looking cervix does not exclude it. The cervical smear is a screening test, not a diagnostic one — persistent PCB or IMB warrants colposcopy / urgent referral regardless of a recent normal smear (see gynaecological cancers). IMB over 40, or with risk factors (obesity, PCOS, tamoxifen, unopposed oestrogen, Lynch syndrome), needs endometrial assessment (TVUS + biopsy) to exclude endometrial hyperplasia or cancer. Do not attribute abnormal bleeding to a benign cause (an ectropion, a pill) until malignancy and pregnancy have been excluded.

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Postmenopaus:
Postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) — any vaginal bleeding occurring 12 months or more after the last menstrual period — is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Around 1 in 10 women with PMB have endometrial cancer, so every case needs urgent (2-week-wait) referral (see gynaecological cancers). The commonest benign cause is atrophic vaginitis, but that is a diagnosis made only after malignancy is excluded (see menopause & fertility). Other causes include endometrial hyperplasia, endometrial or cervical polyps, cervical cancer and HRT-related bleeding (see benign uterine conditions). The key investigation is a transvaginal ultrasound of endometrial thickness, with endometrial biopsy when it is thickened. Watch for risk factors for unopposed oestrogen exposure. PMB may come with discharge (see PV discharge).
🚨Treat all postmenopausal bleeding as endometrial cancer until proven otherwise — refer urgently (2-week-wait). The first-line test is a transvaginal ultrasound: an endometrial thickness > 4 mm mandates endometrial sampling (Pipelle biopsy ± hysteroscopy) (see gynaecological cancers). Do not attribute PMB to atrophy or HRT without excluding malignancy. Risk factors for endometrial cancer reflect unopposed oestrogen — obesity, tamoxifen, PCOS, nulliparity, late menopause, oestrogen-only HRT and Lynch syndrome. Also consider cervical, ovarian (oestrogen-secreting) and vulvovaginal cancers (see menopause & fertility).

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Pelvic Pain:
Pelvic pain in women spans acute emergencies and chronic disability — and the first step in any woman of reproductive age is a pregnancy test. The acute can’t-miss diagnoses are ovarian torsion, ectopic pregnancy and pelvic inflammatory disease (see ovarian torsion, early pregnancy complications, pelvic inflammatory disease), alongside ovarian cyst accidents (rupture or haemorrhage). Chronic pelvic pain is most often endometriosis or adenomyosis, and overlaps with non-gynaecological causes — appendicitis, UTI and irritable bowel syndrome (see benign uterine & pelvic conditions, irritable bowel syndrome). Characterise the pain as acute vs chronic and cyclical vs constant, and always assess the pregnancy status. Pelvic pain overlaps with painful periods and deep pain with sex (see dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia).
🚨Do a pregnancy test, and think torsion, ectopic and PID. Ovarian torsion — sudden severe unilateral pain with an adnexal mass and vomiting — is a surgical emergency: prompt detorsion can save the ovary (see ovarian torsion). A positive test with pain and bleeding is an ectopic until proven otherwise (see early pregnancy complications). PID — pain, deep dyspareunia, discharge, cervical motion tenderness and fever — must be treated empirically on a low threshold to protect fertility (see pelvic inflammatory disease). And never forget appendicitis as a non-gynaecological cause of right-sided pelvic pain (see acute appendicitis).

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Pelvic / Adn:
A pelvic or adnexal mass may be felt on examination or found on a scan — the central question is whether it is malignant. The can’t-miss diagnosis is ovarian cancer, which is more likely when a mass is complex or solid, in a postmenopausal woman, with ascites and a raised CA-125 (a high Risk of Malignancy Index) (see gynaecological cancers). Most masses are benign — functional ovarian cysts, uterine fibroids, endometriomas and dermoids (see benign uterine & pelvic conditions). Always do a pregnancy test: an adnexal mass with a positive test is an ectopic pregnancy, and a central mass may be a gravid uterus (see early pregnancy complications). Any ovarian mass can undergo torsion (see ovarian torsion); consider a non-gynaecological (bowel) mass too (see abdominal mass).
🚨Ovarian cancer is the can’t-miss diagnosis, and every ovarian mass risks torsion and rupture. Suspicious features are a complex / solid / multilocular mass, postmenopausal status, ascites, bilaterality and a raised CA-125 — combined in the Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) to guide gynae-oncology referral (see gynaecological cancers). Vague symptoms (bloating, early satiety, abdominal distension, appetite / weight loss) are the classic red flags of ovarian cancer and are easily dismissed. Always exclude pregnancy: an adnexal mass with a positive test is an ectopic (see early pregnancy complications); and a painful mass with sudden severe pain may be torsion (see ovarian torsion).

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Severe Vomit:
Nausea and vomiting affect most pregnancies; the task is to spot when it becomes hyperemesis gravidarum and to exclude dangerous causes. Hyperemesis gravidarum is the severe end — the triad of > 5% pre-pregnancy weight loss, dehydration and electrolyte disturbance, with ketosis (see medical disorders in pregnancy). It is driven by hCG, so think of a molar or multiple pregnancy when vomiting is extreme (see early pregnancy complications, multiple pregnancy). Give thiamine to every woman needing rehydration to prevent Wernicke’s encephalopathy, and use saline rather than dextrose alone (see Wernicke’s encephalopathy). Always exclude non-obstetric mimics — UTI, DKA and thyrotoxicosis (see pyelonephritis, nausea & vomiting).
🚨Give thiamine, use saline (not dextrose alone), and provide VTE prophylaxis. In a woman with prolonged vomiting, rehydrating with dextrose before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke’s encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia) (see Wernicke’s encephalopathy). Correct hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia and monitor for refeeding. Extreme vomiting suggests a very high hCG — look for a molar or multiple pregnancy (see early pregnancy complications). Do not anchor on pregnancy: exclude diabetic ketoacidosis, pyelonephritis, thyrotoxicosis and, in later pregnancy, pre-eclampsia / HELLP and acute fatty liver (see hypertensive disorders of pregnancy). Hyperemesis carries a raised VTE risk — give prophylaxis.

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Dysmenorrhoe:
Dysmenorrhoea is painful menstruation — the key division is primary versus secondary. Primary dysmenorrhoea has no underlying pathology: it is prostaglandin-mediated, begins 6–12 months after menarche, affects younger women, and the crampy suprapubic pain starts with the flow and eases over 1–3 days (see menstrual disorders). Secondary dysmenorrhoea arises from pelvic pathology, typically presenting later, with pain that precedes the bleed or is present between periods: think endometriosis and adenomyosis, fibroids (see benign uterine & pelvic conditions), pelvic inflammatory disease (see PID) and a copper IUD (see intrauterine device). Always exclude pregnancy and ask about deep dyspareunia (see dyspareunia), discharge and menorrhagia (see heavy menstrual bleeding) that flag a secondary cause.
🚨Painful periods are common and usually benign, but do not anchor on “primary dysmenorrhoea” and miss a secondary cause. Pelvic inflammatory disease with pelvic pain, discharge, deep dyspareunia and cervical excitation threatens fertility — treat empirically and swab (see PID). In any woman of reproductive age, exclude pregnancy: a positive test with pain is an ectopic until proven otherwise (see early pregnancy complications). Sudden, severe, unilateral pain with an adnexal mass may be ovarian torsion — a surgical emergency (see ovarian torsion). Red flags for secondary disease: onset well after menarche, non-cyclical or worsening pain, subfertility, abnormal bleeding, or an abnormal pelvis.

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Postpartum B:
Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) is an obstetric emergency — blood loss of >500 mL after vaginal delivery (>1000 mL after caesarean, or any loss causing haemodynamic compromise). Primary PPH occurs within 24 hours; secondary PPH from 24 hours to 12 weeks postpartum. The causes are the four Ts: Tone (uterine atony — the commonest), Trauma (genital-tract tears, uterine rupture), Tissue (retained placenta or products) and Thrombin (coagulopathy). Resuscitate along A–E lines while finding and treating the cause (see postpartum complications). Secondary PPH is usually retained products or endometritis (see puerperal sepsis). Massive loss causes haemorrhagic shock (see shock); give anti-D to rhesus-negative women.
🚨PPH kills through delay. Call for senior obstetric and anaesthetic help immediately, give oxygen, gain two large-bore cannulae, cross-match, and start uterotonics while resuscitating. Uterine atony is the commonest cause — a boggy, poorly contracted uterus: “rub up” a contraction, empty the bladder, give oxytocin / ergometrine / carboprost and bimanual compression (see postpartum complications). Give tranexamic acid early. If bleeding continues despite a contracted uterus, look for trauma or retained tissue. Sudden collapse with a non-palpable fundus + a mass at the introitus is uterine inversion.

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Puerperal Fe:
Puerperal fever is a temperature ≥38°C in the puerperium (the 6 weeks after delivery) — the task is to find the source and to recognise maternal sepsis early. The classic source is the genital tract (endometritis — offensive lochia, a tender bulky uterus) (see postpartum complications), but a systematic search covers the breasts (mastitis, abscess), wounds (caesarean or perineal), the urinary tract (UTI / pyelonephritis), the chest and the legs / lungs (VTE can present with fever — do not miss PE) (see pulmonary embolism), and retained products. Puerperal genital-tract sepsis, especially from group A streptococcus, can deteriorate alarmingly fast — treat as sepsis and act on the Sepsis 6.
🚨Maternal sepsis is a leading cause of direct maternal death and the signs can be subtle until collapse. A recently delivered woman who is unwell, feverish (or hypothermic), tachycardic, tachypnoeic or hypotensive needs the Sepsis 6 within the hour — cultures, lactate and urine output, then oxygen, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and fluids (see Sepsis 6, source control). Group A streptococcal genital-tract sepsis is the classic rapidly-lethal cause — severe abdominal pain, diarrhoea and vomiting, and shock out of proportion. Look for retained products and secondary PPH (see postpartum bleeding), and remember VTE / PE can masquerade as fever.

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Postnatal Mo:
Postnatal mood disturbance spans a spectrum from a self-limiting normal reaction to a psychiatric emergency — the job is to place the mother on that spectrum and assess risk. The baby blues are common (∼50–80%), start around day 3–5 and resolve within two weeks with support alone. Postnatal depression is a depressive episode, typically emerging over the first weeks to months, that persists >2 weeks and impairs function (see depressive disorders) — screen mood (see low mood). Puerperal (postpartum) psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with rapid onset, often in the first 2 weeks: confusion, mania, delusions and hallucinations, with real risk to mother and baby (see psychosis). Always assess suicide and infanticide risk (see self-harm & suicidal ideation).
🚨Puerperal psychosis is an emergency — it develops fast and carries a risk of suicide and infanticide. Rapid-onset confusion, elation or depression, delusions or hallucinations in the early puerperium needs urgent psychiatric assessment and admission, ideally to a mother-and-baby unit (see schizophrenia / psychosis). A previous history of bipolar disorder or puerperal psychosis is the strongest risk factor. In every mother with low mood, ask directly about thoughts of self-harm and of harming the baby and act on the risk (see self-harm & suicide risk). Do not dismiss persistent symptoms as “just the blues” — the blues resolve by two weeks.

Suspected rupture of membranes is a “my waters have broken” presentation — confirm the rupture, date the gestation, and screen for the two dangers: cord prolapse and infection. Distinguish mimics — urinary incontinence and discharge (see urinary incontinence).
🚨After the membranes rupture, cord prolapse is the emergency that must be excluded — especially with a high or malpresenting part. A palpable, pulsating cord or a sudden fetal bradycardia after rupture is cord prolapse: relieve pressure on the cord (manual elevation / knee–chest or left-lateral position) and arrange immediate delivery (see intrapartum emergencies). Chorioamnionitis — maternal fever, tachycardia, a tender uterus, offensive liquor and fetal tachycardia — is intrauterine infection needing antibiotics and expedited delivery (see infections in pregnancy). Do not perform a digital examination in suspected PPROM without labour, and give corticosteroids if preterm.

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Menopausal S:
Menopausal symptoms are the effects of falling oestrogen — not a disease to be endured. The core clusters are vasomotor (hot flushes, night sweats), urogenital (vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urinary urgency and recurrent UTI — the “genitourinary syndrome of menopause”), and psychological / sleep (low mood, anxiety, poor concentration, insomnia) (see menopause & fertility). Over 45 the diagnosis is clinical — FSH is only needed if under 45 or the picture is atypical. The management question is HRT: benefits versus risks. Crucially, postmenopausal bleeding is a separate red-flag presentation and must never be attributed to “the menopause” — it is worked up to exclude endometrial cancer (see postmenopausal bleeding). Exclude mimics of flushing / sweats — thyrotoxicosis (see hyperthyroidism), phaeochromocytoma, anxiety (see anxiety) and drugs — before attributing everything to oestrogen deficiency.
🚨Postmenopausal bleeding is cancer until proven otherwise — not menopause. Any bleeding ≥12 months after the last period needs a 2-week-wait referral, transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial biopsy (see postmenopausal bleeding). When prescribing HRT, a woman with an intact uterus must have a progestogen — unopposed oestrogen causes endometrial hyperplasia and cancer (see gynaecological cancers). Counsel the small increased risks of VTE (use transdermal oestrogen if at risk) and breast cancer (combined, duration-dependent), and screen contraindications (oestrogen-dependent cancer, undiagnosed bleeding, active VTE). Consider premature ovarian insufficiency if under 40 — it needs HRT to at least the natural age of menopause.

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Subfertility:
Subfertility is failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse — investigate earlier (6 months) if the woman is 36 or over, or there is a known cause. Always assess both partners: causes split roughly evenly between female and male factors. Classify as primary (never conceived) or secondary (previous pregnancy). Female causes are ovulatory (PCOS is the commonest — also hypothalamic, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid, POI) (see PCOS), tubal / pelvic (PID / chlamydia, endometriosis, adhesions) (see pelvic infections) and uterine (fibroids, polyps) (see benign uterine conditions); the male factor is an abnormal semen analysis. Around a quarter are unexplained. The three baseline tests are a mid-luteal (day 21) progesterone for ovulation, a semen analysis, and tubal assessment; then refer for specialist management (see menopause & fertility).
🚨Do not just wait — fertility is age-critical. Ovarian reserve falls sharply after 35, so investigate after 6 months (not 12) if the woman is 36 or older, and refer early if there is a known problem (see menopause & fertility). Consider premature ovarian insufficiency (amenorrhoea + high FSH <40) — refer urgently (see amenorrhoea). Do not miss serious underlying causes: a pituitary tumour (amenorrhoea + galactorrhoea + a bitemporal visual field defect) (see galactorrhoea), and in men a testicular tumour or undescended testis — always examine the testes (see testicular lump). Check rubella immunity and start folic acid preconception.

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Vulval Itch:
Vulval itch or a vulval lump is a presenting complaint that hides a can’t-miss cancer among common benign causes. The two lesions you must not miss are vulval carcinoma — a persistent lump, ulcer, plaque or bleeding, typically in older women, referred on a 2-week-wait pathway (see gynaecological cancers) — and lichen sclerosus, a pre-malignant white atrophic dermatosis (see benign vulvovaginal conditions). Also think of dermatoses (eczema, lichen planus, psoriasis, contact dermatitis), infestations (scabies / pubic lice) (see anogenital itch) and ulcerative STIs (see genital ulcer). The rule: examine every vulva, and biopsy anything persistent or suspicious.
🚨A persistent vulval lump or ulcer in an older woman is vulval cancer until proven otherwise. Do not treat “thrush” blindly for weeks — examine and biopsy any persistent lesion and refer on a 2-week-wait pathway (see gynaecological cancers). Lichen sclerosus is pre-malignant (~5% lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma): white, crinkled, atrophic plaques with intractable itch and scarring — treat with a potent topical steroid and keep under review (see benign vulvovaginal conditions). Any new or changing pigmented vulval lesion may be a melanoma. When itch is the only symptom and swabs are negative, think a dermatosis rather than infection.

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Vaginal Prol:
Vaginal (urogenital) prolapse is descent of the pelvic organs into the vagina — the patient feels “something coming down” or a dragging vaginal bulge, worse on standing or straining. Name the compartment: cystocele (anterior wall / bladder), rectocele (posterior wall / rectum), uterine descent, and vaginal vault prolapse after hysterectomy (see urogenital prolapse). Symptoms cross all three systems: urinary (incomplete emptying, stress incontinence) (see urinary incontinence), bowel (obstructed defecation, splinting) and sexual (see dyspareunia). It is graded on the POP-Q system. First-line care is conservative — pelvic floor muscle training, weight loss and a vaginal pessary — with surgery for those who fail or decline it (see urogenital prolapse). Red flags are ulceration / bleeding of an exposed prolapse and urinary retention / obstructive uropathy.
🚨A complete, exposed prolapse (procidentia) can obstruct the urinary tract and ulcerate. Watch for acute urinary retention or obstructive uropathy — hydronephrosis and acute kidney injury — and catheterise / image (see acute urinary retention). An exposed prolapse may develop a decubitus ulcer that bleeds; reduce it and keep it moist, but never attribute vaginal bleeding to the prolapse without excluding malignancy — a mass or ulcer may be a tumour (see gynaecological cancers). Distinguish a true prolapse from a pelvic / adnexal mass pushing down (see pelvic / adnexal mass).

OBSTETRIC / GYNAECOLOGICAL__Premenstrual:
Premenstrual symptoms are cyclical physical and psychological symptoms of the luteal phase that resolve with menstruation, leaving a symptom-free follicular phase. Physical features include bloating, breast tenderness and headache; psychological features include irritability, low mood, anxiety and tension (see menstrual disorders). Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is the severe end — marked affective symptoms with significant functional impairment, diagnosed on DSM-5 criteria. The key discriminator is timing: true PMS / PMDD is confined to the luteal phase, so a prospective symptom diary over two cycles is the diagnostic test. Symptoms that persist across the whole cycle are a primary psychiatric disorder — depression (see depressive disorders) or anxiety (see anxiety & stress-related disorders) — and a premenstrual exacerbation of an existing disorder is common. Consider perimenopause as an age-related mimic (see menopause & fertility).
🚨PMDD can carry real risk — screen for self-harm and suicidal ideation, which may peak premenstrually. Severe cyclical despair, irritability and loss of control need urgent support and effective treatment (see self-harm & suicidal ideation). Do not mislabel a primary psychiatric disorder as PMS: symptoms that continue throughout the cycle point to depression, an anxiety disorder or bipolar disorder (see depressive disorders), and a bipolar diagnosis matters before starting an antidepressant. The way to tell them apart is a prospective 2-cycle symptom diary — retrospective recall is unreliable. Exclude a thyroid disorder or anaemia contributing to cyclical fatigue.
